title: Breaking the channel barrier: same-fluorescence, different-Tm probe strategy enables seven-target respiratory virus detection on a six-channel PCR platform within 20 minutes.
abstract: BACKGROUND Respiratory pathogens with overlapping symptoms-including SARS-CoV-2, influenza A/B, H5/H7/H10 avian influenza, and RSV-co-circulate and co-infect, demanding rapid multiplex screening at points of care. Conventional multiplex real-time PCR is constrained by hardware channel capacity (≤6), making it difficult to detect seven targets while distinguishing influenza A and B in a single tube. This work addresses the contradiction between high-order multiplexing and limited fluorescence channels without sacrificing speed or sensitivity. RESULTS We developed a six-channel ultra-fast PCR platform detecting seven respiratory viruses in a single tube within 20 min, using a same-fluorescence, different-Tm probe strategy. Influenza A and B share the FAM channel yet generate distinct melting peaks (∼12 °C difference, 84.8 °C vs. 72.3 °C), enabling accurate typing via melting curve analysis. Primers, probes, and enzymes are pre-embedded as lyophilized beads in sealed cartridges for fully automated sample-to-result operation. The assay achieved 100% detection at 5 copies/test for all targets, linearity (R2 > 0.95) across 5-105 copies/test, 90-110% efficiencies, and no cross-reactivity against 39 non-target pathogens. Cartridges remained stable for 12 months at 25 °C. Validation on 271 clinical specimens showed 100% agreement with sequencing-verified single-plex qPCR. SIGNIFICANCE AND NOVELTY This work provides the first integration of melting-curve-based same-channel multiplexing with lyophilized cartridge technology on an ultra-fast PCR platform. By overcoming channel limitations while maintaining speed and sensitivity, the system offers a practical, field-deployable screening tool for decentralized respiratory pathogen detection in resource-limited settings.

title: A prospective, comparative cohort analysis of influenza antibody waning in Michigan and Hong Kong during periods of low influenza circulation
abstract: Background: Reduced influenza transmission during the COVID-19 pandemic prompted concern about waning of population immunity that could lead to subsequent surges in circulation. We compared longitudinal influenza antibody titers in Michigan and Hong Kong, two regions with reduced influenza transmission during the COVID-19 pandemic. Methods: In two prospective cohort studies (HIVE, Michigan; EPI-HK, Hong Kong), we analyzed longitudinal serum samples collected from 2020 through 2023 from participants without influenza infection or vaccination. Sera were tested using hemagglutination inhibition assays (HAI) and microneutralization (MN) against vaccine strains. Two-year fold changes in titers were estimated using multivariable power-law models adjusted for age and baseline titer. Results: We analyzed 173 sera from 57 HIVE participants and 259 sera from 60 EPI-HK participants. Initial HAI geometric mean titers ranged from 12.3-123.4 in HIVE and 6.3-40.9 in EPI-HK. Among those with >1:40 baseline titers in HIVE, fold-change estimates indicated waning for H1N1 strains, including A/Brisbane (0.70 [95% CI: 0.56,0.86]), A/Idaho (0.40 [0.32,0.50]), and A/Michigan (0.43 [0.34,0.52]), while H3N2 and influenza B showed minimal or no waning. In EPI-HK, fold-change estimates demonstrated heterogeneous patterns by strain for H1N1, and waning for selected H3N2 strains, including A/Cambodia (0.44 [0.29,0.65]) and A/Singapore (0.48 [0.33,0.69]). MN results were consistent with HAI findings. Conclusion: Influenza antibody responses during the pandemic showed heterogeneous, strain-specific changes rather than uniform decline. These findings suggest that population immunity was maintained for many strains despite reduced viral circulation, with waning occurring in particular strains and varying by population.

title: Lossless Reductions and Hybrid Sampling for Phylogeny Using the Maximum Compatibility Criterion
abstract: Maximum compatibility provides a criterion for phylogenetic reconstruction in which the objective is to retain a maximum set of mutually compatible characters. For binary characters, pairwise compatibility can be represented by a weighted graph whose vertices correspond to characters and whose edges connect compatible pairs. A leading algorithm by Cherry [BMC Bioinformatics, 18(1):127, 2017] uses this representation to identify maximum compatible character sets as maximum weight cliques. We formulate the problem as maximum weight independent set enumeration on the complement graph and use deterministic postprocessing to map sampled bit strings to maximal feasible solutions. To explore the prospects of quantum computational advantage, we further construct bespoke correction-in-the-loop Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm instances and find that traditional Lagrange multiplier choices may not be optimal for the enumeration problem on noisy devices. We also introduce lossless graph reductions with reconstruction rules that preserve the complete set of optimal solutions. Our results indicate that graph reduction and sampling can be effectively combined to address the enumeration bottleneck in maximum compatibility phylogeny, while retaining exact reconstruction when the residual optimum set is completely resolved. We enhance Cherry's approach to maximum compatibility by introducing graph reduction techniques and quantum sampling. Our classical benchmarks show a clear difference between finding one optimum and recovering the optimum set in practice. We demonstrate the utility of our methods on graphs constructed from SARS-CoV-2 sequences.

title: Adaptación de Etiquetados de Exportación Bajo una Estrategia de Aprendizaje Colaborativo Internacional en Línea (COIL)
abstract: The internationalization of higher education demands the implementation of innovative teaching techniques and strategies that promote collaborative learning and foster the development of global competencies. Education underwent a radical shift as a consequence of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic; therefore, information technologies played a crucial role by enabling online classes from home. It was then that this new experience of international collaborative learning, known as Collaborative Online International Learning (COIL), began to emerge. This article describes a COIL learning experience developed by undergraduate students in Mexico and Colombia, whose main objective was to identify the applicable regulations in each country in order to design and adapt labels and technical specifications for local products destined for international markets. The methodology employed in this research is descriptive with a qualitative approach, based on the development of this teaching practice. The experience unfolded over four weeks with synchronous virtual sessions and asynchronous collaborative activities, facilitating interaction between teachers and students. This allowed for the analysis of national and international legislation related to product labeling, resulting in innovative proposals that will enable the future marketing of the product in the partner country. The results demonstrated the strengthening of intercultural, technological, and disciplinary competencies, as well as an understanding of international trade regulations. It was confirmed that the COIL methodology serves as an effective strategy to promote curriculum internationalization, foster meaningful learning, and encourage virtual mobility in higher education institutions.

title: A novel proviral mechanism for the ISG, Shiftless, during human coronavirus infection
abstract: As highly pathogenic human coronaviruses continue to emerge from zoonotic sources, understanding how host intrinsic immune responses control infection is critical for preventing severe disease. The interferon (IFN) pathway induces antiviral effectors, including the interferon-stimulated gene (ISG) Shiftless (SHFL), which restricts -1 programmed ribosomal frameshifting during SARS-CoV-2 infection. Here, we investigate a novel proviral mechanism for SHFL using loss-of-function and gain-of-function approaches. Despite its established antiviral activity, SHFL enhanced infection by SARS-CoV-2 and the seasonal coronavirus HCoV-229E by increasing cellular susceptibility to infection. SHFL further promoted coronavirus infection by reducing cellular sensitivity to IFN, potentially through modulation of JAK/STAT signaling. Finally, we demonstrate that SHFL-mediated enhancement of baseline viral susceptibility is partially dependent on the domain previously implicated in its antiviral inhibition of -1 programmed ribosomal frameshifting. In contrast, SHFL-mediated regulation of IFN signaling is independent of this domain. Together, these findings establish SHFL as a dual-function ISG with distinct proviral and antiviral activities, highlighting the complex roles of innate immune effectors during coronavirus infection.

title: Sample overlap in genome-wide association meta-analysis: practical comparisons across significance thresholds
abstract: Meta-analysis is widely used in genome-wide association studies (GWAS) to combine evidence across studies without requiring individual-level data. However, as both the number of studies included in meta-analyses and their sample sizes continue to grow, the same participant may be included in more than one study. Such sample overlap induces dependence across studies and violates the independence assumptions underlying standard meta-analysis methods. HostSeq is a Canadian initiative in which 15 clinical and epidemiological studies were assembled with DNA samples from approximately 10,000 Canadians infected by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. We observed duplicate samples across different participating studies. This observation raises an important practical question: what is the impact of sample overlap on association results, and when should such overlap be a concern? Motivated by this real problem, we sought to compare five meta-analysis methods and evaluate their performance against a reference mega-analysis in which the true sample overlap is known. We show that when the degree of sample overlap is relatively small, its impact on association results is minimal, even at the genome-wide significance threshold of = 5*10 -8 . We demonstrate these findings through extensive simulation studies and an application to overlapping cohorts within HostSeq.

title: CAPO: Compute-Aware Automated Protein-Model Optimization
abstract: Protein models such as Evolutionary Scale Modeling (ESM), AlphaFold and Boltz have transformed computational protein science, yet a pretrained model rarely transfers to a particular laboratory's assay without adaptation to its data and experimental setting, and that adaptation is technically demanding and spends real compute budget. Existing agentic systems can automate model training, yet typically treat fine-tuning as a reliable tool call: feasibility and cost are estimated rather than measured, and infeasibility is discovered only after compute has been spent. We formulate protein-model adaptation as a gated decision problem: given a task, raw data and a compute budget c_max, a system should decide whether and how to adapt a model before committing expensive computation. We introduce CAPO (Compute-Aware Automated Protein-Model Optimization), a multi-agent system built around one rule: gate before you train. CAPO measures feasibility on the target accelerator, projects cost against the available budget, runs a canary inside the actual training loop and maintains an auditable artifact trail; critically, it can decline an unaffordable adaptation and select a cheaper alternative. We evaluate CAPO, without system changes, on three protein-modeling tasks: (i) SARS-CoV-2 host-range prediction, (ii) hit-to-lead affinity ranking and (iii) temporal variant-effect reclassification. On host range, CAPO partially fine-tuned an 8-million-parameter ESM-2 model to a species-averaged MCC of 0.826, compared with 0.743 for a hand-designed expert transformer; it matched a general coding agent while using 57.4% less GPU time and reduced failed training trials from four to zero. For hit-to-lead affinity ranking, CAPO rejected Boltz-2 fine-tuning and instead trained an assay-calibrated lightweight head over frozen representations, improving ranking on 11 of 15 held-out targets in 1.68 GPU-hours. On temporally held-out ClinVar variants, rank-4 low-rank adaptation of ESM-2 reached an MCC of 0.478, compared with 0.252 for a one-hot baseline and 0.000 for the frozen zero-shot score. These results come from single runs, without a gate ablation and with one generalist-agent comparison. Within those limits, they show that measured admission control can make protein-model adaptation not only automated but selective: deciding what to compute, what not to compute and why.

title: Clonotype specificity distinguishes epitope-tailored and permissive somatic hypermutation
abstract: Identifying antibody features that reliably encode epitope specificity poses a major barrier towards modeling antigen-antibody interactions. Affinity maturation offers a unique opportunity to probe the molecular basis of antigen-antibody interactions by revealing how individual somatic hypermutations (SHM) refine antibody binding. Using SARS-CoV-2 spike-specific germinal center B-cell repertoires, we show that antibodies harboring multiple SHMs that are restricted to their respective clonotypes (clonotype-restricted SHMs) preferentially recognize cryptic epitopes. We structurally characterized three such antibodies: two recognized a cryptic epitope on the receptor-binding domain whereas a third bound an N-terminal domain epitope that is almost entirely occluded in prefusion spike. In contrast, SHMs shared across multiple clonotypes using the same V gene recur across antibodies targeting diverse antigens but generally fail to enhance affinity when introduced into diverse antibody backgrounds. Together, these findings define a spectrum of SHM behavior, distinguishing epitope-tailored mutations from broadly recurrent but largely permissive substitutions.
